name: The Hellenistic Age as a distinct period
plain_explanation: Russell divides Greek antiquity into three phases: free but disorderly city-states (to Philip/Alexander), Macedonian domination marked by subjection and disorder (the 'Hellenistic' age proper), and finally Roman rule, which brought subjection but also order. The Hellenistic age is the middle phase.
precise_definition: The period from Alexander's conquests (334-323 B.C.) to the final Roman absorption of the Macedonian successor kingdoms (ending with Egypt in 30 B.C.), during which Greek culture spread across a vastly enlarged, politically fragmented world under Macedonian dynasties.
why_it_mattered: It is the incubator of Epicureanism, Stoicism, and formal Scepticism, and of the diffusion of Greek science; it also prepared, in Russell's view, the psychological ground for Christianity by turning philosophy toward individual salvation.
historical_origin: Begins with Alexander's campaigns of 334-324 B.C. against the Persian Empire.
examples: The Ptolemaic kingdom of Egypt and its capital Alexandria
The Bactrian Greek kingdom under Menander
influence_on_later_thinkers: Sets the social conditions (loss of civic power, chronic insecurity) that Russell says produced the individualist, salvation-oriented philosophies of the Cynics, Sceptics, Epicureans, and Stoics discussed in the following chapters.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political: it is defined by the transition from city-state self-government to dynastic empire.
